html:
The moai are the giant stone figures carved by the Rapa Nui people on Easter Island, in the far east of Polynesia, between about 1250 and 1500. More than 900 are known.

Rapa Nui was one of the last places reached in the settlement of East Polynesia, and one of the most remote inhabited islands on earth. Its settlers carried Polynesian beliefs about chiefs and ancestors with them. The moai are the "living faces" of deified ancestors. Most stood on stone platforms called ahu near the coast, looking inland over the land of the clan that raised them.

Facts about them:

  • Nearly all were carved from volcanic tuff at the quarry of Rano Raraku, where almost half still lie, some unfinished in the rock.
  • They have oversized heads, about three-eighths of the whole figure, and no legs.
  • The tallest one erected, Paro, was almost 10 metres high and weighed about 82 tonnes.
  • Many wore pukao, topknots of red stone.

How they were moved is still argued. Rapa Nui tradition says the statues "walked", and experiments have shown that teams with ropes can rock an upright moai forward.

When the Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen arrived on Easter Sunday 1722, the moai were standing. By the later 19th century all had been pulled down, in wars between clans or in the upheaval after European contact. Peruvian slave raids in the 1860s and disease then nearly destroyed the population. A once popular story of self-inflicted "ecocide" is now disputed by many archaeologists. The island's undeciphered rongorongo script is another puzzle it keeps.
sum: The moai are the giant stone figures carved by the Rapa Nui people on Easter Island, in the far east of Polynesia, between about 1250 and 1500. More than 900 are known.
